deleted.text: Every list endpoint is paginated by page number.
A client sends `page_number`, starting at 1, and `page_size`, between 1 and 100.
Every response carries the `X-Total-Count` header with the number of items in the whole filtered collection.
A request that omits `page_size` receives 25 items, and a request that omits `page_number` receives the first page.
Filters and the sort order are passed as ordinary query parameters and must be repeated unchanged on every request of a traversal.
The server computes the offset as `(page_number - 1) * page_size` and skips that many rows of the sorted collection before reading the page.
`items`
array
The items of the requested page, in sort order
`page_number`
integer
The page the server returned
`page_size`
integer
The page size the server applied
The `X-Total-Count` header is present on every successful response, including an empty one.
The `page_size` field echoes the size the server applied, which may be lower than the one requested under load.
Each endpoint sorts by a stable key, by default creation time followed by item id.
Endpoint authors may offer other sort keys, but every key must end with the item id so that the order is total.
An item created or deleted ahead of the current position during a traversal shifts every later item by one place.
A client walking the pages may therefore see an item twice or miss one.
Clients that need an exact copy deduplicate by item id and repeat the traversal when `X-Total-Count` changed between the first and the last page.
A `page_size` above 100 or below 1 receives 400 Bad Request with the error code `invalid_page_size`.
A `page_number` past the last page receives 200 with an empty `items` array and the usual `X-Total-Count` header.
A `page_number` above 1000 receives 400 with the error code `page_too_deep`, because deep pages force a long scan.
Filters that differ from those of the first request are not detected, and the client receives pages of a different collection.
Clients may fetch several pages in parallel, since each page is addressed by its number alone.
A user interface that offers numbered page links sends the chosen `page_number` directly.
Progress bars divide `X-Total-Count` by `page_size` to know how many requests a full traversal takes.
Clients that only need the size of a collection request one item and read the header.
A request for page n costs the database a scan of roughly n times the page size rows before it reaches the first returned item.
Computing `X-Total-Count` costs one count query per request, cached for 30 seconds per filter combination.
Rate limits count requests, so a client that asks for 100 items per request uses its quota most efficiently.
Endpoint authors keep an index that covers the default sort key and every filter they expose.
The official SDKs wrap traversal in an iterator that increments `page_number` until a page holds fewer items than `page_size`.
The iterator retries a request once on a network error and then raises.
The SDKs also expose a `count()` helper that requests one item and returns `X-Total-Count`.
The mobile SDK fetches up to four pages in parallel to fill a feed quickly.
Whether the depth cap should be raised for export jobs.
The data team has asked for 5000 pages.
Whether `X-Total-Count` may be approximate for collections above a million items.

candidates.sentence: A client sends `limit`, between 1 and 200, and, on every request after the first, the `cursor` value taken from the `next_cursor` field of the previous response.
A response without `next_cursor` is the last one of the traversal.
A client no longer works out where the next request starts from the number of the page it is on and the size of each page.
Our cursors carry no such promise, and their contents may change in any release without notice.
The server never returns more items than the limit the response reports.
Responses carry no X-Total-Count header, so progress bars have to be sized some other way.
The sort key is chosen from the list the endpoint publishes, not composed by the client as a free-form expression.
An unreadable cursor is reported as an error, never silently taken as a request for the first items.
A request that repeats a cursor already followed receives the same items again, as long as the cursor has not expired.
Jumping straight to an arbitrary point in the middle of a collection is not something clients can do any more.
The API cannot serve that request yet, and no response carries a cursor for the preceding items.
